The body of water that Minneapolis (the city where The Minikahda Club is located) sits on is the **Mississippi River**.

# Visiting the Club
Thank you for visiting The Minikahda Club.
Our policies are designed to ensure every member and guest experiences a welcoming, respectful, and memorable visit. Rooted in more than 127 years of tradition, they reflect the values that have guided the Club since its founding in 1898 along the shores of Bde Maka Ska: family, fellowship, integrity, and respect. From its origins as a gathering place for Minneapolis pioneers of golf to hosting six USGA championships and welcoming tennis legends such as Andre Agassi, Minikahda has preserved the traditions and standards that define its legacy, from the iconic Donald Ross golf course and historic Greek Revival clubhouse to its celebrated racquet and recreational offerings.
By following these policies, we honor the Club’s heritage while maintaining an environment of courtesy, consideration, and refined hospitality. They allow every member and guest to appreciate the distinctive experience Minikahda provides, from the serene vistas of the lake to the quiet reverence for tradition that permeates the Club.
With guidance on areas such as dress, personal conduct, and the use of Club facilities, these policies help maintain the distinguished and welcoming atmosphere that has defined Minikahda for over a century, ensuring all who visit feel comfortable, valued, and at ease.
For your convenience, complimentary valet service is offered at the Clubhouse entrance. Self-parking is available in the main parking lot. For further assistance, please contact the Club Concierge at [612-926-1601](tel:6129261601).

# Visiting the Club
## Visiting the Minikahda Club
The Minikahda Club is located at 3205 Excelsior Boulevard, Minneapolis, MN 55416. The map provided will guide you to the main Clubhouse; should your visit be for another property on the grounds, the Club Concierge will guide visitors to the intended property at [612‑926‑1601](tel:6129261601). Guests may park in the main parking lot or use the roundabout for valet service. All guests should check in with the Club Concierge upon arrival. The Concierge is pleased to provide guidance, answer questions, and ensure a seamless visit befitting the distinguished hospitality of Minikahda.

#
### minikahda club
Minneapolis, Minnesota
**Golf Course Practice Range Renovation**
**PROJECT PROFILE**
The Minikahda Club is one of Minnesota’s oldest and most prestigious
golf courses. The course was originally designed by Willie Watson,
who also designed Interlachen Country Club, and Robert Foulis. The
course has since undergone numerous renovations including work by
Thomas Bendelow and Donald Ross. Improvements have included
repositioning of greens, lengthening of holes and, more recently, the
extensive removal of trees and complete the reconstruction of over 100 sand bunkers.
The existing rangewas too narrow, too short and had insufﬁcient teeing area. Recommendations included incorporating the reconstruction of the
existing tennis course area and parking lot in order to balance soil requirements, address Minnehaha Creek Watershed requirements and to minimize construction costs. The new range includes a 40,000 square foot practice tee, artiﬁcial turf teeing area, target greens, new state of the art irrigation system, short game practice facility and two practice sand bunkers.
**RESPONSIBILITIES**
Herfort Norby was responsible for all aspects of
the project including preparation of detailed plans,
watershed and City permitting, bidding, contractor
selection and construction administration.

# The Minikahda Club
## Overview
Something was in the air in Minneapolis and St. Paul in the 1920s. Call it an _esprit de refaire_(French for “repair”). Many of the prominent clubs in the market looked at their existing golf courses and thought, “we can do better.” The Twin Cities were an incubator for the first major movement of golf course reformation as courses laid out just years before by designers like Tom Bendelow, William Watson and Willie Park, Jr., were redesigned, most of them by Donald Ross. Interlachen (No. 1), White Bear Yacht Club (No. 4), The Club at Golden Valley (No. 15), Minneapolis G.C. and others. The Minikahda Club also falls into this category. Robert Foulis designed the original nine, and Watson was involved in some capacity, too. Then the club hired Donald Ross to completely revamp the course after Chick Evans dismantled the old design in the 1916 U.S. Open, shooting a then-record 286 using just seven clubs. Many more renovations ensued, but the club has perhaps settled on a lasting version after the work of Kyle Franz, who continued a program of thinning overgrowth, widening fairways and recreating bunker shapes and arrangements reminiscent of the club’s 1920s heyday.

“I love the location by the lake. The first, 5th, 15th, 16th, 17th, and 18th are all shortish fun par 4s. Wind presents challenges. The middle of the course is the hardest part. Ross at his best."

2025
3 / 6
“Great membership that was friendly and welcoming. Excited to share their course. Wonderful rolling hills and rumpled fairways though your ball would tend to end up in common areas judging by the amounts of divots. The course drains well so you did get roll and firmness but you can tell they use a ton of water to keep it 'Augusta Green' complete with white sand bunkers. MN is currently finishing up an extremely dry summer. The greens were the highlight. Every green contained multiple contours which allowed you to be creative but also needed to have a delicate touch. Unfortunately, because of the amount of water used, the greens were soft and the course is on the short side so someone dialed in with their wedges is going to have lots of looks at birdie. You did not have to worry about hard bounces kicking you over the green. Lots of straight holes with very few feeling like repeats which is impressive. A couple of the par threes are basically the same hole."
Read More  
2023
4 / 6

# The Minikahda Club
## Review
“Wonderful Kyle Franz renovations of this Ross gem, in particular the green surround of 13. Surprisingly long and difficult from holes 2-16 for this age of course. Firm and fast conditioning yet fair throughout the round other than 9 green. The 9th green site was a little unfair based on this panelist's observations....very difficult to one or two putt and not have a 40-50yd pitch up the hill coming back as well as the wedge shot or pitch coming into the green if one is in the fairway not spinning back off the green. Unique to have three par 3's and three par 5's on the front nine with only one par 3 on the back 9. Seemed to test all the clubs in your bag at the end of the day, another rarity for this age of course."
Read More  
2023
6 / 6
“Had the great pleasure of playing it shortly before they hosted the US Sr. AM. Great condition and a wonderfully fun design. Fantastic clubhouse and great setting right on the water. Condition was near perfect."

# The Minikahda Club
## Overview
Something was in the air in Minneapolis and St. Paul in the 1920s. Call it an _esprit de refaire_(French for “repair”). Many of the prominent clubs in the market looked at their existing golf courses and thought, “we can do better.” The Twin Cities were an incubator for the first major movement of golf course reformation as courses laid out just years before by designers like Tom Bendelow, William Watson and Willie Park, Jr., were redesigned, most of them by Donald Ross. Interlachen (No. 1), White Bear Yacht Club (No. 4), The Club at Golden Valley (No. 15), Minneapolis G.C. and others. The Minikahda Club also falls into this category. Robert Foulis designed the original nine, and Watson was involved in some capacity, too. Then the club hired Donald Ross to completely revamp the course after Chick Evans dismantled the old design in the 1916 U.S. Open, shooting a then-record 286 using just seven clubs. Many more renovations ensued, but the club has perhaps settled on a lasting version after the work of Kyle Franz, who continued a program of thinning overgrowth, widening fairways and recreating bunker shapes and arrangements reminiscent of the club’s 1920s heyday.
